summary:
The reflection of light is an important phenomenon that helps us see objects in the world around us. When we look at something shiny, like a spoon, our eyes receive reflected light from it. This reflected light travels to our eyes and allows us to see the object.

A spherical mirror is an example of a reflecting surface that can form a part of a sphere. It has two main parts: the pole, where the reflecting surface forms a part of a sphere, and the centre of curvature, which lies outside the reflecting surface. The radius of curvature of the mirror determines how much light is reflected by the mirror.

When we look at a concave mirror, like a spoon, our eyes receive reflected light from it. This reflected light travels to our eyes and allows us to see the object. However, if we move the spoon slowly away from our face, the image formed on the curved surface of the spoon appears inverted. This is because the light rays that hit the curved surface are bent by the mirror.

The reflection of light can also be affected by the shape of the reflecting surface. A convex mirror has its reflecting surface curved outwards, which means it bends light in a different way than a concave mirror. When we look at a convex mirror, our eyes receive reflected light that is bent and appears distorted.

The laws of reflection are also important to understand when studying the phenomenon of reflection. The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, normal to the mirror at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane. These laws help us understand how light behaves when it hits a reflecting surface.

The size of the image formed by a spherical mirror depends on the distance between the object and the mirror. The image is always virtual and erect, and its size is equal to that of the object. The image appears to be behind the mirror as long as the object is in front of it.
